findings.text: The fragments expose several global code symbols for cross file use while keeping paired return helpers file local. The global set seen here comprises a paranoid state preservation entry, a fault entry dispatcher, a nonmaskable interrupt entry, an ignored 32 bit system call target, a branch history clearing routine and a compatibility SYSENTER target. The paranoid exit and fault return sequences are local, indicating they are reached only by nearby entry code.

The paranoid helper establishes a safe kernel context for faults that may interrupt either privilege level or an in progress entry sequence. It preserves the general register file with return address handling, records address space state for verbatim restoration, moves to kernel address space before touching kernel segment state so table based segment lookup works, then establishes kernel segment base through a feature dependent path, applies speculation controls and return retraining, validates safe return from interrupt context and returns to its caller.

Segment base handling has two modes selected by processor capability. When modern segment base instructions are available the entry unconditionally saves the current base and installs the kernel base, and the exit unconditionally writes back the saved value. When unavailable a flag records whether kernel base was already active by probing the sign of a segment base register value; negative means kernel base needs no switch, otherwise a base swap is done on entry and undone on exit, with speculation fences around the switch.

Address space and speculation state follow a strict nesting order. Entry stashes prior address space identity in a callee preserved register and switches early. It saves speculation control only after address and segment state are usable. Exit restores speculation first because it needs per CPU data reachable through kernel segment state, then restores stashed address space while still on kernel segment state, then restores segment state. The paranoid exit never handles faults from user mode; those use the fault return path.

The fault entry dispatcher branches on privilege encoded in the saved code segment. From user privilege, or from a fault pretending user privilege after a failed return to user, it swaps segment base with fencing, moves to kernel address space, engages speculation defenses and retraining, then transfers to a common register synchronization path with a pointer to the saved register area. From kernel privilege it falls through to kernel fault classification and returns a register area pointer directly.

Kernel privilege faults are classified by saved instruction pointer. A match against the normal interrupt return location indicates a failed return to user and redirects to a bad return fixup that reinstalls kernel segment and address state and synthesizes a user mode fault frame. A zero extended match covers a truncated return address erratum on a specific stepping and is repaired before taking the same path. A match against a known segment update location indicates a fault with user segment base and is repaired by swapping base before fencing and accounting call depth.

The paired fault return helper selects its return mechanism from privilege encoded in the saved code segment, after asserting interrupts are disabled. It resumes kernel execution through a kernel register restore path when saved privilege is kernel and through a segment swapping user restore path otherwise.

The nonmaskable interrupt entry splits sharply by interrupted privilege. From user privilege it swaps segment base with fencing, switches address space and stack to the per CPU top of thread stack without pushing before the switch, copies the five element hardware frame to the new stack, marks no system call for restart, preserves registers, engages speculation defenses and calls the high level handler with a register area pointer, then returns directly to user mode without normal exit work so interrupts stay disabled.

While on the dedicated nonmaskable stack the kernel mode path maintains contiguous zones for the hardware supplied return context, scratch storage, a flag recording whether a handler is already active, a mutable return copy that a nested arrival may rewrite to request repetition, a stable outermost copy preserved for the whole handling loop, and the saved register area. Return uses a single interrupt return reading the mutable copy, which either leaves the stack or loops back for another iteration.

Nested arrivals are detected by three ordered tests. An interrupted address inside the repetition window means the outer handler is already preparing another iteration so the inner arrival resumes it without touching shared frames. Otherwise a set active flag means nesting. Otherwise the prior stack pointer is compared against dedicated stack bounds; inside bounds plus direction set means true nesting while direction clear means user controlled stack at system call entry and is treated as outermost. Nested arrivals rewrite the mutable return copy to force repetition and return immediately.

The outermost handler initializes the stable copy from hardware state, marks active on each iteration, refreshes the mutable copy from the stable copy outside the window where nested writes are forbidden, then invokes paranoid entry and the high level handler and unwinds speculation, address and segment state in paranoid order. It restores registers, skips the restart marker and stable copy to point at the mutable copy, sets direction before clearing active so the clearing window is distinguishable from system call entry, and exits with one interrupt return to kernel mode.

The ignored 32 bit system call target provides a minimal end of stack entry that reports operation not implemented in the result register, clears CPU buffers for speculation hygiene and returns with a fast 32 bit system return.

The branch history clearing routine preserves frame pointer and runs a small nested counting loop with internal calls and returns placed to control cache line position, followed by a load fence before restoring frame pointer and returning.

The compatibility SYSENTER target runs with interrupts disabled and builds a full register save area on the per CPU top of thread stack. It swaps segment base, switches address space, pushes placeholder stack and instruction values with user data and 32 bit code segment selectors plus saved flags, zero extends the system call number, records it as the original operation while marking the result as not implemented, preserves remaining registers, clears direction, sanitizes status flags, engages speculation defenses and branch history clearing, then calls the 32 bit dispatcher with a register area pointer and continues to the 32 bit system return path.

Status flags from SYSENTER are sanitized before interrupts can be enabled because the instruction does not filter them. A test for nested task, alignment check or trap being set diverts to an out of line fix that loads a fixed flag image and rejoins the main path; this keeps single step behavior predictable and prevents preemption with nested task set. Speculation helpers run only after trap handling is settled.

Several hazards motivate fencing, ordering and special cases. Mispredicted segment base loads around swaps, residual branch history and CPU buffers across privilege transitions, and return misprediction after entry require fences, buffer clearing and retraining. Concurrent nonmaskable arrivals can corrupt each others frames, so active flag, stack bound and repetition window checks serialize them. Single stepping through entry, faults during segment updates, failed returns to user and a truncated return address erratum require explicit detection and repair.

Privilege is conveyed in the low two bits of the saved code segment, tested to separate user arrivals from kernel arrivals on fault, nonmaskable and return paths. A restart marker of all bits set denotes no system call to restart in nonmaskable and kernel repetition frames. Segment selectors distinguish kernel code and data from user data and 32 bit user code when building or rewriting return frames. Fault results use negated operation not implemented for unknown 32 bit calls and placeholder zero stack and instruction values in synthesized SYSENTER frames.

Stack and flag encodings seen here include a dedicated nonmaskable stack size used for bound comparison, a per CPU top of stack used to switch from user or nonmaskable stacks to thread stack, a model specific register holding segment base whose sign indicates kernel base on legacy systems, a direction flag used to distinguish handler clearing windows from user controlled stack, and status bits for nested task, alignment check, trap plus a fixed image used for sanitization.
